name: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma
aliases: nodal T-follicular helper cell lymphoma, angioimmunoblastic type

clinicalPearls: Typically affects older adults with generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fever, weight loss, and a characteristic skin rash
Autoimmune-like features are common, including polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia, haemolytic anaemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test, arthralgia, and circulating immune complexes
The neoplastic cell is a T-follicular helper (TFH) lymphocyte expressing CD4 with markers such as CD10, CXCL13, PD-1, ICOS, and BCL6
Nodes show a polymorphous infiltrate, arborising high endothelial venules, and expanded follicular dendritic cell meshworks, which can obscure the malignant clone
Epstein-Barr virus-driven B-cell blasts are frequently present and can occasionally transform into a secondary EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Recurrent mutations affect TET2, DNMT3A, IDH2, and RHOA, reflecting an origin often shared with age-related clonal haematopoiesis
Immune dysregulation predisposes to opportunistic infection, which contributes significantly to morbidity
reference.pathophysiology: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma arises from T-follicular helper cells, a subset that normally supports germinal-centre B-cell responses. Early epigenetic mutations in TET2 and DNMT3A may originate in a haematopoietic stem cell, with later acquisition of RHOA and IDH2 changes driving the malignant TFH phenotype. The tumour recreates an aberrant germinal-centre microenvironment, secreting chemokines such as CXCL13 that recruit B cells, plasma cells, eosinophils, and dendritic cells, producing the polymorphous nodal picture. Loss of normal immune regulation explains the prominent autoimmune phenomena, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and reactivation of Epstein-Barr virus in bystander B cells, which can themselves undergo clonal expansion.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive viral lymphadenopathy with immune activation
Other peripheral T-cell lymphomas, not otherwise specified
Classic or nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
Autoimmune disease with lymphadenopathy such as systemic lupus erythematosus
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy with immunohistochemistry for the TFH panel (CD10, CXCL13, PD-1, ICOS, BCL6)
In situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA to highlight bystander B blasts
T-cell receptor clonality studies and often concurrent B-cell clonality assessment
Molecular testing for TET2, DNMT3A, RHOA, and IDH2 mutations where available
Direct antiglobulin test, serum immunoglobulins, and autoantibody screen
Cross-sectional imaging and bone marrow examination for staging
redFlags: Rapid clinical deterioration with high fever suggesting aggressive disease or intercurrent opportunistic infection
Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis such as cytopenias, hyperferritinaemia, and rising triglycerides
Emergence of a rapidly enlarging mass indicating transformation to large B-cell lymphoma
Severe autoimmune haemolysis causing symptomatic anaemia
reference.prognosis: The disease is generally aggressive with a guarded outlook; many patients relapse after combination chemotherapy, and older age, poor performance status, and infective complications worsen outcome, though epigenetic-targeted approaches are under evaluation.
pitfalls: Misreading the polymorphous, inflammatory-appearing infiltrate as reactive or as Hodgkin lymphoma and missing the malignant TFH clone
Attributing systemic symptoms solely to infection or autoimmune disease and delaying biopsy
Overlooking a secondary EBV-driven B-cell proliferation or transformation
Failing to anticipate and prevent opportunistic infection during immunosuppressive therapy
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Confirm diagnosis via excisional lymph node biopsy with a T-follicular helper immunohistochemistry panel, complete staging, and screen for autoimmune and infective complications before starting systemic therapy

A subset of patients have spontaneous remission or remission with corticosteroids alone during work-up; recognize this to avoid over-treating a stabilizing patient, without delaying definitive therapy in aggressive disease
For patients needing systemic treatment, use anthracycline-based combination chemotherapy as first-line induction, following the peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified approach

Consider autologous stem cell transplant consolidation in first remission for younger, fit responders to induction; this is an option, not mandatory, and depends on age, comorbidity, and response depth/durability

In relapsed or refractory disease, follow peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified salvage approaches, reserving salvage chemotherapy plus autologous transplant for selected chemosensitive relapses

Consider non-myeloablative allogeneic transplant in selected relapsed/refractory patients for durable disease control, weighing non-relapse mortality, decided at experienced transplant centers after multidisciplinary discussion

In relapsed/refractory disease, consider histone deacetylase inhibitors, hypomethylating agents, and antifolate therapy (noting antifolate responses are less reliable in AITL than in peripheral T-cell lymphoma generally); consider an anti-CD30 antibody-drug conjugate when the tumor is CD30 positive
Discuss and pursue clinical trial enrollment early in relapsed/refractory disease given generally modest and often non-durable responses to available agents
Use corticosteroids and other immunomodulatory measures to manage autoimmune hemolytic anemia, polyarthritis, and other immune-mediated phenomena independent of anti-lymphoma treatment
Maintain infection prophylaxis and vigilance for opportunistic infection throughout treatment, as this is a recognized cause of death in AITL
Re-biopsy a rapidly enlarging mass or unexplained deterioration to evaluate for secondary EBV-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma transformation rather than assuming AITL progression
Perform response assessment with standard lymphoma restaging imaging after treatment completion, since achieving complete response is the key determinant of longer-term outcome

Provide longitudinal surveillance for relapse, secondary EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma, opportunistic infection, and fluctuating autoimmune phenomena (hemolysis, arthropathy, thyroid dysfunction)

Manage all patients through a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team from diagnosis, with prompt transplant assessment referral, early access to clinical trials for relapsed/refractory disease, and early involvement of palliative and supportive care
